bipartite.kami_theme: The speaker describes rowing out onto the vast sea toward the many islands (Oki), an act of departure into exile
bipartite.shimo_theme: An appeal to the fisherman's boat to carry word of this departure back to people (loved ones/court) left behind
bipartite.pivot_note: The physical act of rowing out into the sea (kami) becomes the occasion and vehicle for the message the speaker begs to have conveyed (shimo) — the boat that carries him away is entreated (via the fisherman who might see him) to also carry news of his fate back to those he leaves behind, turning a scene of departure into an urgent communicative plea across the gap of exile.

kakekotoba.reading_primary: かけて (目指して/towards, heading for)
kakekotoba.reading_secondary: かけて (懸けて, to stake/risk, or to span/extend across)
kakekotoba.interaction: Primarily read as 'heading toward/aiming for' the eighty islands, but carries an undertone of 懸けて, 'staking' or 'spanning across' the vast distance, reinforcing the sense of a perilous, committed crossing into exile.

kigo.word: わたの原・あまのつり舟
kigo.note: The poem centers on the sea, islands, and a fisherman's boat, which are not tied to a specific season in the classical calendar; this is fundamentally a travel/exile poem (a topic outside the four-season kigo framework) rather than a seasonally-marked poem. No blossom, leaf, snow, moon, dew, frost, mist, insect, or seasonal bird term appears; 舟 (boat) and 海人 (fisherman) are conventional imagery of sea life but carry no seasonal charge in the classical canon.
